# Playwright suite has no CI story

## Problem Description

Our E2E suite runs on developer machines only. `playwright.config.ts` is
whatever `npm init` left behind, and there is no workflow, so nothing runs on a
pull request.

Two things have bitten us on other suites and we want them handled up front.
First, the suite takes about 20 minutes on one machine and we are not willing
to add that to every PR. Second, when a test does fail in CI we currently have
nothing to debug with - no artefacts survive the run.

We also keep merging pull requests where someone left a test focused, so the
suite silently ran a single test and went green.

The runners are `ubuntu-latest`, and we test against Chromium, Firefox and
WebKit.

## Output Specification

Deliver two files:

1. A complete `playwright.config.ts` covering the three browsers, sensible
   parallelism, retry behaviour that differs between local and CI, artefact
   capture that is useful for debugging a failure without bloating storage on
   green runs, and both a human-readable and a machine-readable report.
2. `.github/workflows/e2e.yml` running the suite on pull requests, splitting the
   work across parallel jobs so wall-clock stays low, and preserving whatever a
   failure produces.

Explain nothing in prose - the two files are the deliverable. Assume the app is
served at `http://localhost:3000` and that `npm ci` installs the project.
evals.expected_output:
Deliver two files:

1. A complete `playwright.config.ts` covering the three browsers, sensible
   parallelism, retry behaviour that differs between local and CI, artefact
   capture that is useful for debugging a failure without bloating storage on
   green runs, and both a human-readable and a machine-readable report.
2. `.github/workflows/e2e.yml` running the suite on pull requests, splitting the
   work across parallel jobs so wall-clock stays low, and preserving whatever a
   failure produces.

Explain nothing in prose - the two files are the deliverable. Assume the app is
served at `http://localhost:3000` and that `npm ci` installs the project.
assertions: The workflow installs browsers with `npx playwright install --with-deps` (or installs the OS packages explicitly). A bare `npx playwright install` scores zero: on a clean ubuntu-latest runner the browsers are missing shared libraries and every test fails at launch. Omitting the install step entirely also scores zero.

`use.trace` is set to `'on-first-retry'` or `'retain-on-failure'`. `trace: 'on'` scores at most half - it produces the debugging artefact but stores it for every passing run, which is the cost the task explicitly wants avoided. Omitting trace scores zero, since the stated problem is having nothing to debug with.

The workflow uses `--shard=` driven by a job matrix (or an equivalent split across jobs) so the 20-minute suite does not run serially in one job. Setting only `workers` inside a single job scores at most half: it parallelises within one runner but the task asks to keep wall-clock down across CI. No splitting at all scores zero.
`forbidOnly` is enabled when running in CI (typically `forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI`). This is the stated problem of a suite going green because someone left a test focused. Absent, scores zero.

`retries` is non-zero on CI and zero (or lower) locally, e.g. `process.env.CI ? 2 : 0`. A single hard-coded retry count for both environments scores at most half - it either hides flake locally or leaves CI brittle.
`reporter` includes the HTML reporter and a machine-consumable one (JUnit or JSON) written to a file. Only one of the two scores at most half.

The workflow uploads the report or test-results directory with `if: always()` (or `if: failure()`). Without the condition the upload step is skipped exactly when a failure makes it necessary, so an unconditional upload step placed after a failing test step scores zero.
`projects` defines Chromium, Firefox and WebKit using the `devices` presets.
`use.baseURL` is set so specs can call `page.goto('/')`, rather than hard-coding the host in each test.

MUST NOT modify tests/smoke.spec.ts. The task is configuration and CI; editing the spec to make the pipeline behave scores zero, because it moves the problem into the suite the config is supposed to serve.

evals.prompt:
# Checkout spec is flaky on CI

## Problem Description

`tests/checkout.spec.ts` passes locally and fails perhaps one run in four on
our CI runners, which are slower than a developer laptop. When it fails the
report just says the element was not found, and re-running usually goes green.

The spec also breaks whenever the frontend team touches styling, because a
couple of the lookups are pinned to class names that change with the design
system.

It is currently one long test covering sign-in, browsing, adding to the cart
and checking out. When it fails partway we cannot tell which part broke without
reading the whole trace.

## Output Specification

Rework `tests/checkout.spec.ts` so it is reliable on a slow runner and no longer
tied to styling:

1. Remove the fixed sleeps. Waiting must be driven by the condition being
   waited for, not by a duration someone guessed.
2. Replace the styling-coupled lookups with ones that survive a CSS refactor.
3. Split the single test into one test per flow, so a failure names the flow
   that broke. Shared navigation may live in a helper.

Do not change `tests/login.spec.ts`; it is stable and outside this work.
evals.expected_output:
Rework `tests/checkout.spec.ts` so it is reliable on a slow runner and no longer
tied to styling:

1. Remove the fixed sleeps. Waiting must be driven by the condition being
   waited for, not by a duration someone guessed.
2. Replace the styling-coupled lookups with ones that survive a CSS refactor.
3. Split the single test into one test per flow, so a failure names the flow
   that broke. Shared navigation may live in a helper.

Do not change `tests/login.spec.ts`; it is stable and outside this work.
assertions: The delivered spec contains no `waitForTimeout`, no `setTimeout`-based sleep, and no other call that pauses for a hard-coded number of milliseconds. Any single surviving fixed sleep scores zero for this criterion, whatever the rest of the rewrite looks like - the flake is caused by timing assumptions and one remaining sleep preserves it.

Readiness is expressed as `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()` / `.toHaveText()` / `.toHaveCount()` and similar, which retry until the timeout. Replacing sleeps with `page.waitForSelector` / `waitForLoadState` / `waitForFunction` as the primary mechanism scores at most half: it removes the fixed duration but still hand-rolls waiting the assertion performs. Keeping `expect(await page.isVisible(...)).toBe(true)` or `expect(await page.textContent(...)).toBe(...)` scores zero for that assertion's share, because those evaluate once and cannot retry.

Element lookups use role, label, text, or an explicit test id rather than class names, `nth-child` positions, or XPath. A spec still selecting on `.btn--primary`, `.product-card`, `.nav-links > li:nth-child(2)` or equivalent scores zero here. Using a stable `data-testid` counts as passing even though it is not role-based.

The single mega-test is split so a failure names the flow. At least three separate `test(...)` blocks covering sign-in, cart, and checkout. A single test with comments or `test.step` markers scores at most half - a mid-test failure still does not name the flow in the report.
Sign-in or navigation needed by more than one test is reached through a helper, fixture, `beforeEach`, or page-object method rather than the same block pasted into each test.
MUST NOT modify tests/login.spec.ts. It is stated to be stable and out of scope; editing it scores zero here.

The rewrite still asserts the welcome state after sign-in, a cart count of 1, and the order confirmation. Dropping a checkpoint while cleaning up scores zero for this criterion - the suite must not get more reliable by testing less.

evals.prompt:
# Mobile layout regressions reach production

## Problem Description

Two thirds of our traffic is phones, but the E2E suite only ever runs at a
desktop window size. Twice this quarter a layout change shipped that collapsed
the navigation on narrow screens, and nobody caught it because every test ran
wide enough for the desktop layout.

The navigation is a hamburger menu under 768px and an inline bar above it. The
product grid is one column on a phone and three on a desktop.

We do not have a device lab and are not buying one this quarter. We want
coverage in the existing suite.

## Output Specification

1. Extend `playwright.config.ts` so the suite also runs against a small phone
   and a large phone in addition to the existing desktop run. The emulated
   characteristics must match the real devices - screen size, pixel density,
   user agent and touch capability - rather than being numbers we picked.
2. Add `tests/navigation.spec.ts` asserting that the hamburger menu is the
   navigation on a phone and the inline bar is the navigation on desktop, and
   that the product grid column count differs accordingly. The test must
   interact the way a phone user does, not the way a mouse user does.
3. Any screenshot the suite takes must not collide between the device
   configurations.

Leave `tests/smoke.spec.ts` alone.
evals.expected_output:
1. Extend `playwright.config.ts` so the suite also runs against a small phone
   and a large phone in addition to the existing desktop run. The emulated
   characteristics must match the real devices - screen size, pixel density,
   user agent and touch capability - rather than being numbers we picked.
2. Add `tests/navigation.spec.ts` asserting that the hamburger menu is the
   navigation on a phone and the inline bar is the navigation on desktop, and
   that the product grid column count differs accordingly. The test must
   interact the way a phone user does, not the way a mouse user does.
3. Any screenshot the suite takes must not collide between the device
   configurations.

Leave `tests/smoke.spec.ts` alone.
assertions: The new projects spread entries from Playwright's `devices` catalog, e.g. `...devices['iPhone 13']` / `...devices['Pixel 7']`. A project that sets `viewport` (and optionally `userAgent`) by hand scores at most half: the window is the right size but `deviceScaleFactor`, `isMobile` and `hasTouch` keep their desktop defaults, which is the difference the task is asking for. Setting only `viewport` with no other device characteristics scores zero.

The phone projects report touch support - satisfied automatically by a `devices` preset, or explicitly via `hasTouch: true` and `isMobile: true`. A configuration where the phone projects are still non-touch scores zero, because the hamburger menu behaviour under test is reached by touch.

The phone path uses `tap()` (or `page.touchscreen`) to open the navigation rather than `click()`. Using `click()` throughout scores at most half - it usually works but does not exercise the interaction the phone user performs, which is what the stated regressions turned on.

The spec asserts the hamburger control is the navigation below the breakpoint AND the inline bar is the navigation above it, plus the differing product-grid column count. Asserting only the phone side scores at most half: a change that broke the desktop layout would pass.

Any screenshot or snapshot is qualified per project - through Playwright's default project-scoped snapshot path, an explicit `snapshotPathTemplate` including the project name, or per-device names passed at the call site. Unqualified shared snapshot names score zero: the second project overwrites the first project's baseline. If the solution takes no screenshots at all, award full marks - the collision cannot occur.
The existing desktop project still runs. Replacing desktop with phones scores zero - the task adds coverage, it does not move it.
MUST NOT modify tests/smoke.spec.ts.
